speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to present a motion on a matter of pressing and urgent necessity.
Considering the enormous decrease in the employment level in the textile industry in Canada and considering that this is one of the most important industries, in particular in the eastern part of the country because of the policy concerning textile imports which affect our own jobs, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau):
That this House urge the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce to take position openly in favour of the Canadian people who are in the textile industry and to propose to the House a new set of regulations governing textile imports, the first objective being to protect jobs in Canada and have Canadians consume Canadian rather than foreign products, so that our own investments are protected by our legislation.

Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to introduce a motion dealing with an urgent matter of pressing necessity.
Considering the massive use of chemical insecticides in eastern Canada, especially in Quebec, to control the spruce budworm thus seriously threatening the ecological balance and giving rise to disastrous effects since the infestation of our forests by the budworm is increasing in spite of all the

ANTI-INFLATION BOARD GUIDELINES FOR DEALING WITH MEMBERS' COMPLAINTS ABOUT PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance and concerns the report released today that the Anti-Inflation Board is inviting consumer complaints and placing a form in supermarkets and financial institutions for this purpose. Considering the record of the AIB in respect of letters from members of parliament which are not being replied to when we bring price complaints to the attention of the board, and that the best we receive is a phone call saying everything has been looked after without our really knowing what has happened, may I ask the Minister of Finance what guidelines have been laid down by the AIB regarding members' complaints about price increases? If the AIB does not have such guidelines, does the minister have some? What action will the minister take to assure the House that today's announcement is a serious attempt on the part of the AIB to deal with prices and listen to complaints rather than just being another public relations job?
May 18, 1976

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
maintopic: ANTI-INFLATION BOARD GUIDELINES FOR DEALING WITH MEMBERS' COMPLAINTS ABOUT PRICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the guidelines with regard to price increases of course have been set out at length before parliament and are incorporated in the regulations. They will depend directly upon the nature of the business dealings carried on by the firm. But in general with regard to the distribution business, they are related to the gross profit margin of those businesses. With regard to the hon. gentleman's complaint that his letter has not produced a letter, I wish to reflect on that. It seems to me the more important occupation for the Anti-Inflation Board should be in scrutinizing the price questions the hon. gentleman has raised rather than engaging in correspondence.

maintopic: ANTI-INFLATION BOARD GUIDELINES FOR DEALING WITH MEMBERS' COMPLAINTS ABOUT PRICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I sort of anticipated that the minister might be assisting the AIB in its public relations job. I am not interested in the AIB sending out letters or making phone calls. The information I am interested in getting from the minister is whether the Anti-Inflation Board will follow through in some serious way with the complaints that are laid before it or whether it will get some lady or young man on the telephone with a nice voice saying: "Don't worry about it; everything is under control; you can trust us". That is all we have been getting up until now. In asking my question the purpose is not to increase the correspondence between the AIB and members of parliament but to get some documentary evidence of good faith on the part of the AIB that it is following through with suggestions placed before it and is handling them.

maintopic: ANTI-INFLATION BOARD GUIDELINES FOR DEALING WITH MEMBERS' COMPLAINTS ABOUT PRICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am confident that the board is following through, particularly with regard to particular patterns of price increases which indicate a practice in this regard. Indeed, there have been a great many investigations of this kind.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Since ICNAF will be meeting in Havana, Cuba, June 6 to June 24 and the United States will have a 200-mile limit by March 1, 1977, is it the minister's intention to soon meet with U.S. delegates to see whether a common front can be established concerning how ICNAF may be changed?

subtopic: STATEMENT ON NUCLEAR CO-OPERATION WITH INDIA

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT ON NUCLEAR CO-OPERATION WITH INDIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to inform the House that the government has decided that further nuclear co-operation with India is not possible.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON NUCLEAR CO-OPERATION WITH INDIA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT ON NUCLEAR CO-OPERATION WITH INDIA
speechtext:
The decision has been difficult. It has challenged the government, as indeed it has challenged all thinking Canadians, to review a number of fundamental principles.
Canada's nuclear co-operation with India began in the context of the Colombo Plan. It has, as its basis, the belief that nuclear power could be vital to the equitable economic growth of a number of developing countries. The energy crisis and the serious dislocations it has brought with it have tended to reinforce this belief, and the genuine success achieved by Indo-Canadian co-operation in the development of nuclear power for energy, agriculture and medicine has proved the practicality of this approach.
India's detonation of a nuclear explosive device in 1974 made it evident that Canada and India have taken profoundly differing views of what should be encompassed in the peaceful application of nuclear energy by non-nuclear weapons states. Canada is one of the earliest and most vigorous proponents of the nuclear non-proliferation treaty. A basic element of the treaty, which guides Canadian policy in the field of nuclear exports and safeguards, is that it recognizes no technical distinction between nuclear explosives for peaceful and non-peaceful purposes.
Canada has forgone the possible benefits of developing so-called peaceful nuclear explosions on the basis that, pursuant to the NPT, nuclear explosive services would be available from a nuclear weapons state at such time as need and feasibility are demonstrated. India, however, does not accept what it views as discrimination between the nuclear powers and other states and insists that all countries should be free to use all phases of nuclear technology for whatever they view as peaceful purposes.
Notwithstanding these differences, both countries agreed to explore together a negotiated termination of nuclear co-operation. These negotiations had, earlier this spring, reached a point where both sides decided that governmental decisions were required. The decision now taken by cabinet takes into full account the issues that I raised when I spoke in the House on March 23. Canada has insisted that any co-operation in the nuclear field be fully covered by safeguards which satisfy the Canadian people that Canadian assistance will not be diverted to nuclear explosive purposes. This Canadian objective could not be achieved in these negotiations.
Both sides have made a concerted effort in good faith to reach a basis for agreement. However, the Canadian government has decided that it could agree to make new nuclear shipments only on an undertaking by India that Canadian supplies, whether of technology, nuclear equipment or materials, whether past or future, shall not be used for the manufacture of any nuclear explosive device. In the present case, this undertaking would require that all

May 18, 1976
Nuclear Relations with India
nuclear facilities, involving Canadian technology, in India be safeguarded. We would be prepared to reach agreement with India on this basis only. In view of earlier discussions, however, we have concluded that the Indian government would not be prepared to accept safeguards on other than the RAPP reactors, which are already under international safeguards.
In making this statement regarding our nuclear co-operation with India, I should like also to refer briefly to the other aspects of our relationship. There is no question that our nuclear differences are profound; nevertheless, nuclear affairs form only one part of what has been a broad and important relationship. The decisions reached by the government relating to one aspect of our relations are not intended to preclude the pursuit of other elements of mutual interest in our over-all links with India. The Canadian government remains prepared to review these elements and to pursue our common objectives in both bilateral and multilateral fields because we feel that our ties with this important developing Commonwealth nation must not be allowed to lapse through any lack of will on our part.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON NUCLEAR CO-OPERATION WITH INDIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister's statement today is one small step toward a world policy of nuclear sanity, and for this reason we welcome it. Our party, and indeed many Canadians from all walks of life, believe that a moratorium on the export of nuclear technology is imperative until such time as world conditions are more stabilized and countries are willing to accept the authority of a transnational institution with the power to protect the global environment. The Canadian government has by no means implemented such a policy today. But we must hope that the cancellation of the nuclear agreement with India will lead to a reassessment of our current and prospective agreements with other nuclear purchasers.
We need to know precisely why the negotiations with India were terminated and we call on the government to table the relative papers. Without them we cannot judge the real reason for the breakdown. On March 23 the minister posed the dilemma that Canada faced in these terms:
Would it be better for us to suspend completely the nuclear negotiations with India, or should we go on to complete current negotiations, applying to the prospective deal the strictest sanctions possible-
We believed then, and we believe now, that the moral dilemma was falsely posed by the government. For as General E. L. M. Burns, the respected head of Canadian disarmament teams has said so often, it is the Canadian government's duty to do nothing which may lead to the proliferation of nuclear weapons, and that this obligation-which is explicit in article III of the non-proliferation treaty-takes precedence over Canada's desire to assist, through nuclear technologies, the underdeveloped nations of the world.
I think that the many members who have initiated debate from this side of the House can take some credit for this decision. In particular, this House owes a debt of gratitude to the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) who has for the last two years pressed home this matter in parliamentary debate and in the question period. No one

should be under the illusion that this decision has been achieved without much effort both on the part of members of this House and individuals outside it. Yet while we applaud this first step we must realize that it is only that. This decision does not, in itself, form a moral policy with regard to nuclear sales. We still have far to go before our policy measures up to current United States legislation in this area.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON NUCLEAR CO-OPERATION WITH INDIA
speechtext: And British legislation.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON NUCLEAR CO-OPERATION WITH INDIA
speechtext:
Parliament still has no control over sales, as does the U.S. Congress. Parliament is not even consulted; it is merely informed. Unlike Congress, which has had the opportunity to mould the formation of U.S. policy on safeguards, parliament has been pushed aside. As William Epstein, a Canadian who formerly served as chief of the United Nations secretariat on disarmament, said:
Canada, as is its practice, held no public inquiry or committee investigation into the problem. It heard no experts other than its own government employees with no opportunity for them to be heard in public. The debate in parliament was all too short and of insufficient depth for such a serious and complicated matter.
I might add that debate was called by the opposition making use of the scarce resources of parliamentary time available to it. I can only quote the leading saint in the Liberal pantheon, Mackenzie King, who nearly 50 years ago-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT ON NUCLEAR CO-OPERATION WITH INDIA
speechtext: You were in that pantheon.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON NUCLEAR CO-OPERATION WITH INDIA
speechtext:
And I quickly got out of it. Mackenzie King said, nearly 50 years ago:
Parliamentary approval should apply where there are involved political considerations of a far-reaching character.
Those words are in Hansard for April 12, 1928. What could be more far-reaching than nuclear proliferation, a horror undreamed of at that time?
We must also recognize that although this decision will, hopefully, have very far-reaching moral implications, it will have little impact on India's nuclear program. I understand that the RAPP II station is 85 per cent complete and that the Indian department of atomic energy will be able to finish it, albeit behind schedule. India is now completely self-sufficient in nuclear power; therefore, we are a decade too late to change that.
I should like to close with a few questions for the hon. gentleman. Will he now release the agreement initialled by Mr. Head in India? How will this decision affect the rest of our nuclear exports program? Finally, what was the precise point of difference between India and Canada which could not be resolved?

subtopic: STATEMENT ON NUCLEAR CO-OPERATION WITH INDIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my party also welcomes the government's decision. We think it is a fairly small step in the direction of nuclear sanity, to use some of the words of the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner). I suppose one can say that there is more joy in heaven if but one sinner repents.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: STATEMENT ON NUCLEAR CO-OPERATION WITH INDIA
speechtext: Ask Mackenzie King.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON NUCLEAR CO-OPERATION WITH INDIA
speechtext:
There may yet be hope. The decision is a small step in the direction of a sane over-all nuclear policy.
May 18, 1976

The decision, as the minister said in his statement, has challenged all thinking Canadians to review a number of fundamental principles. Yet we are concerned since other fundamental principles have not been reviewed; they have been given only cursory consideration. The present decision relates to only one arrangement with India. That is not enough to give the Canadian people any confidence in a nuclear policy which does not lend itself to an appalling proliferation.
We have had two years to examine the problems of India. However, within that time we have also had the opportunity to agonize over South Korea, Argentina, Pakistan and Taiwan. What this decision really shows is the impossibility of preventing diversion, short of some absolute control process, short of an international agreement in which there is a minor degree of the surrender of sovereignty so that an international agency has the power to enforce an international agreement. Anything short of that does not give reassurance to the nations of the world.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON NUCLEAR CO-OPERATION WITH INDIA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: STATEMENT ON NUCLEAR CO-OPERATION WITH INDIA
speechtext:
Canada has an opportunity to provide moral leadership on this subject. It should be the first nation to go to the United Nations and make that kind of an offer in order to try and snowball other nations to move in the direction of internationalism. There would then be some confidence that the awesome risk of terrorism or unstable governments having control of the nuclear trigger would be reduced or eliminated.
As the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe said, the moral dilemma that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) posed is phony and false. I want to add some support to that. The United States called for a special study in terms of the nuclear program under the energy research and development administration. I want to quote from that study in terms of the need for less developed countries having the nuclear option. This is what they found after very extensive research:
There are no truly compelling economic reasons for a vast commitment to nuclear power in lesser developed countries. There are other ways to develop more consistent with the history, their culture, economics, that are just as efficient. Military power and national prestige are the big causes of the nuclear choice for the LDC.
Therefore, it is not a moral dilemma that we should risk the question of proliferation against the need to peddle peaceful nuclear reactors in the way we have been peddling them. We have been peddling them like used cars, without any sense of responsibility in terms of a peaceful world. I want to again quote General Burns. This is a recent quote from the Globe and Mail:
Once CANDU reactors are built, and producing plutonium, there will be nothing to stop an Argentinian or South Korean government abrogating the inspection agreement, and proceeding on the road to "peaceful nuclear explosions".
That is exactly the dilemma we faced with India, and exactly the dilemma we will be faced with in spite of the agreement with South Korea. In spite of all the pieces of paper the minister can table in this House, those agreements can be abrogated. There is not a sanction in the world to prevent it. Once they are abrogated, these countries can go into what they euphemistically call peaceful
Nuclear Relations with India
nuclear explosions. They then become a part of the nuclear problem, having the nuclear trigger in their hands.
It is time for a nuclear policy that says no more sales abroad, a total moratorium, and a meaningful offer at the United Nations as the first country willing to give up a piece of sovereignty in terms of a world of sanity and safety.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON NUCLEAR CO-OPERATION WITH INDIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, obviously the only role a country such as ours can play is to set an example for peace and thus prevent anything that could be interpreted as military action. Of course, we agree with the decision contained in the minister's statement because we cannot participate, particularly directly, in any endeavour which might have dire consequences.
Mr. Speaker, that reminds me that as a country dedicated to bring peace in the world we should stop any trade which could be the cause of conflicts or wars. And one of the examples we should set is to avoid arming ourselves.
Of course, we should finally understand that given Canada's low density of population spread over such a vast territory as ours, it is quite ridiculous to arm ourselves as much as we do. And it is also ridiculous to see that such huge amounts of money are spent for our national defence.
So not only should we refrain from supplying arms to other countries but we should also seriously think of reducing significantly our expenses for our defence.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON NUCLEAR CO-OPERATION WITH INDIA

fer of technology. However, it is my understanding that that technology is now available to India. It is because we were unable to safeguard all installations, including the Madras reactors, the Cirus reactor and a further new reactor proposed by India, that we decided we could not go further.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON NUCLEAR CO-OPERATION WITH INDIA

May 18, 1976

original production of nuclear weapons and who was later president of many important organizations such as the TVA in the United States, together with our own General Burns-who has been twice mentioned here already-have both expressed the view that the very best safeguards we have devised are inadequate and that they can be evaded fairly easily, would the hon. gentleman accept the principle put forward by my hon. friend from New Westminster that Canada should be willing to limit its sovereignty by accepting, as far as CANDU is concerned, complete and effective international inspection and control of all nuclear installations?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT ON NUCLEAR CO-OPERATION WITH INDIA
speechtext:
I believe that in terms of the nuclear proliferation treaty Canada has done precisely that. All nuclear installations in Canada are under the inspection system of the International Atomic Energy Agency. We have limited our sovereignty. Under the terms of the treaty we have renounced the undertaking of explosions, so to speak, and we have opened all our facilities to NPT inspection. It seems to me there comes a point at which any particular country, after making some solemn undertaking-as we have done-can, acting on its own, abrograte those undertakings. That applies to all forms of international law. The world has not yet devised a system of enforcement that will overcome the problem posed by any country that abrogates its international undertakings. Nothing the hon. member for New Westminster said provided a solution to that problem.
To undertake to limit your sovereignty is binding for the duration of the period that you live up to your commitment and not a moment beyond. We have no international force that I know of that can enter a country with armed forces and say, "You must now live up to your international commitment". Is that what the hon. member is advocating?

Capital Punishment

['Mr. Speaker, this is the fourth time I have taken part in and listened to debates in the House on this subject. It is not an easy decision to make. I think everyone has to ask himself; What is my position? He should then set it out immediately. My position is somewhat refined, in a sense, since I am a partial retentionist. I believe some form of capital punishment should be retained, and I ask hon. members to bear with me when I say "some form". Too often the principle is confused by consideration of the method of execution for planned, premeditated murder where conviction is based on direct evidence rather than on circumstantial evidence. There are many such cases and I shall refer to them.
With regard to this type of offence, I say there should be no exception. On the other hand, the Criminal Code provides for commutation in certain circumstances, and in exceptional cases where there is doubt or where any uncertainty arises at the trial-and it is always difficult to get a new hearing-it is possible for the cabinet to commute sentences, but this procedure should be used properly and always in accordance with the law.', "May 18, 1976
Capital Punishment
I have in the past supported the idea that the death penalty should apply in the case of the murder of a police officer or prison guard. I also support the idea that it should apply to all persons convicted of premeditated, planned murder in cases where the verdict is based on direct evidence. Under the former terms of the Criminal Code there is a division between capital murder and noncapital murder. From my experience, I can say that defence counsel would tell the jury, before any evidence had been presented either by the Crown or by the defence, that much of the evidence to be presented would be circumstantial in nature, and in such cases the accused would be tried only on the charge of non-capital murder. I believe that system worked very well. I believe the death penalty should also apply in cases where a person is found guilty of treason, by which I mean treason in its real sense, the undermining of the country by unlawful insurrection, and that it should also apply in the case of the assassination of the monarch.
This afternoon, my right hon. friend from Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) directed a question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) with reference to the abolition of capital punishment for treason, the unlawful overthrow of the government of Canada, or the assassination of the monarch. He stated in the preamble to his question that it might be very difficult for some abolitionists to vote for a bill which contained no provision for capital punishment in such cases. I do not think anyone who knows my right hon. friend would question his philosophy on this subject-we all know where he has stood with regard to it over the years. But this is an aspect which he has questioned.
I would call the attention of the government to the fact that we are living in times when violence is on the increase, when it does seem that violent groups can get together. I do not know whether the stories we have read recently with respect to threats to the Olympics is an exaggeration or not, but we do know what happened on another occasion when the Olympics were held. I suppose the answer given by the Prime Minister was the best he could do under the circumstances. He said, to paraphrase his words, that there should not be exceptions made in particular cases. Well, Mr. Speaker, I would remind you and other members of the House that on the three occasions in recent times when this subject has been discussed in the House, he himself voted for the provision of exceptions; he voted in favour of the application of capital punishment in particular cases. In other words, on those three occasions the issue before the House was not complete abolition; it was partial abolition and partial retention.
The government undertook to give that arrangement a trial for five years. Now, 2M>
years later, we are at it again. I would point out, though, that the right hon. gentleman has commuted all the sentences passed by the courts since he became minister of justice and prime minister of the country. The situation in Canada has been one of abolition de facto, if not de jure. Members of the government have flaunted the law which they themselves developed and which was agreed to upon a vote in this chamber.
The position of the Progressive Conservative party, without any evasion or equivocation whatsoever, is that all

our members will have complete freedom of thought and action in respect of this highly controversial and emotional matter. There will be no direction given to our members by our leader. All of us will speak freely as individuals and will vote freely. On the other hand, when asked whether members of the Liberal party will be given the opportunity to vote freely, both the Prime Minister and the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) wiffle and waffle before finally admitting that though the whip will not be on as far as ordinary members of parliament are concerned, it will certainly be on for members of the cabinet.
The excuse given is that since this is a government bill, it must be supported by the cabinet. Let us consider this proposition. The government could easily make it clear that whatever way the vote should go-in particular, should it go against the government, in support of retention-it would not constitute a vote of non-confidence in the government. Then Liberal members of the cabinet as well as those on the backbenches could vote freely. Not only is there control in the sense that 27 members of cabinet will not be allowed a free vote, but influence is effectively used in other ways. In an article written during the days when this party formed the government, the prime minister talked about the power to appoint parliamentary secretaries. They were told to toe the line.
Mr. Speaker, I see it is five o'clock. I will continue my remarks after supper."]

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE

speechtext: The House resumed, from Friday, May 14, consideration of the motion of Mr. Allmand that Bill C-84, to amend the Criminal Code in relation to the punishment for murder and certain other serious offences, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday I had just begun my few remarks concerning this bill. I intend to be fairly brief. I have listened very carefully to many other members who have preceded me, many of whom have had a great deal of experience in this House and others who are here, as I am, for the first time following the last election. Let me say I have respect for all sides of the question. I have found little I can criticize, and I am not prepared to challenge others for their points of view as to whether capital punishment should be restored or should be abolished. It is necessary for me, I believe, to answer this question for myself in a free and open way, and it is for me to state my case so that those in my riding will have a clear understanding of what I have to say on this issue. I do not intend to question the statistics put forward by others, and in no way do I wish to call them into account. I am sure all hon. members have attempted to be honest and fair in their approach and in informing their constituents of the facts as they see them and as they have researched them.
I found it very difficult, as I imagine other members did, to answer the tremendously important question: Do I represent myself, or my constituents who elected me, in the free vote on this bill? Indeed, it will be a free vote on this side, and I think that will be evident when two people who work as closely together as myself and the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) vote differently on this matter, as I am sure we will. This will clearly indicate that no instructions have come from the whip on this side, nor from the leader of our party. We have been enjoined to review the situation and to vote as free members of this House on the basis of conscience.
As to the matter of representing my constituency, I have taken this very seriously. It is an honour to attempt to follow the example of many other members of the House, particularly those of my own area around Hamilton, Brantford and the Pensula municipalities, whether they be members of the Liberal party, the Conservative party or the NDP. I have noted how carefully and how sincerely they have made their decisions and showed an interest in the feelings of their ridings. I have tried in some way to imitate them because I do feel that imitation is the most sincere form of flattery. If I come out of this as well as they have in making up their minds, I will feel honoured and will at least be able to look at myself in the mirror.
The constituency I represent is a very interesting one. I have asked myself how my constituents think in respect of this issue. I have done all the normal things, including sending out surveys. I made certain my constituents

May 18, 1976
Capital Punishment
received an every-constituent mailing which indicated to them the details of the peace and security package, without any editorial comment, just the details of the bill. At the same time, I assured them I would listen to them at open meetings, would meet with them in supermarkets, as I came out of the church, on the streets, and at sporting events: I would listen to what they had to say to me on this matter.
I set the stage for them to comment by setting forth the peace and security package of this government which contained the bill which first of all attempted to give peace of mind to the Canadian public, a public which at this moment seems to be very fearful of what is happening on our streets. The peace and security package indicated that our law enforcement agencies are important and that it may be unfortunate that we send people to prison, but that we felt we must in some way give the Canadian public adequate protection. Also, in proposing the legislation concerning the licensing and holding of guns we attempted to say, not that we could deal with the criminal element but at least in some way we might prevent some of the tragedies which occur because of the possibility that people handling weapons might use them in a way to hurt those they love.
It is my belief that through bail reform and our efforts to deal with prisoners, rehabilitation and parole-making certain parole is earned, and not automatic-we are saying to the Canadian public that this is the moment we are strongly behind our law enforcement agencies which serve us so well, and this is the moment we are strongly behind our courts in an attempt to give adequate security to the people.
If it is correct that we are providing this kind of security to Canadians, then at this time we recommend this bill which would once and for all put aside the death penalty as a means of punishment in respect of capital murder, substituting instead a penalty which would confine the convicted person to prison for a period of time to ensure that he or she will not be a danger on our streets. This is the context in which we have talked about abolishing capital punishment.
The bill concerning the peace and security package is now before the committee, where amendments can be made if it falls short of what we require and is not acceptable to certain people in Canada. We are now debating the principle on second reading of the capital punishment issue. I have heard from the people in my riding, having received about a 14 per cent reply to my survey and having listened to the people on the street, but I cannot say only what was contained in those replies to my survey. I cannot say just what somebody said to me in the supermarket. I cannot say just what somebody said to me coming out of church. I have now to reply in some informed way concerning what I believe is the best way I can serve my constituency and the Canadian public for the benefit of all concerned at this moment in casting my vote.
I believe that when I talk about my constituency it is like holding up a mirror. I have to hold a mirror up to them to indicate to them what they see themselves as. If I hold up the wrong image, then they will say that I do not know

my constituents. What is the image I see: what do I see in that mirror of Hamilton Mountain? I see a group of people who enjoy living in a community which is part of the larger community of Hamilton and is part of a large province, Ontario, which is a province of Canada. But although they are citizens of the world, they feel very much part of Hamilton Mountain as an area served by its own small newspaper, served by its own cable TV, and an area that has its own junior Fincups although they were for all of Hamilton in the Memorial Cup.
This is an area which has its own recreational areas, its own churches and its families living and joining together among the various ethnic groups. This is the Hamilton Mountain I know. I know there are some people there who would say that we must retain capital punishment because this is the only way we can deal with the ultimate crime. I know there are others who would speak out and say no, who would say they are for the right of life theory, the theory of the right of children, the right of man and woman, the right of the aged, and therefore the right to life. So when I hold up the mirror, all those images come forward and now I must try to interpret how I can best serve all my constituency, remembering that included with that fine community, ultimately, is Ontario, Canada and possibly the world.
We must remember that poisonous weeds bloom well in prison air. We have to remember the simple thought that the people in prison sometimes nurture the foulest and most evil thoughts. Very little good grows within prison. When those who are in prison see the person who is described as the one who killed the thing he loved, knowing that all hope is taken from this person, knowing that this person now must indeed dance the dance that has no floor, knowing that this person will have his life taken, they find that quite often something dies in them, too. Something in them dies in respect of their feeling for society. Something in them is completely gone when they think about a society which will not take upon itself responsibility for the evil that exists and which will not accept its own face in the mirror, but will take a life and say, "There; it is solved and gone".
I have to say, for my side of it, that I cannot believe that. I believe that all men in some way kill the thing they love. Some, as it is said, do it with a bitter word, some use flattery, and some use a kiss. All of us share in any crime that exists in society. There is no need to ask for whom the bell tolls, for indeed it always tolls for thee or me. I am involved in mankind. I have no right to be a peninsula, sitting all alone. I am part of a society which kills. I am part of a society which takes life. I do not want a state which decides it will use that right. I do not want capital punishment to be legalized, even if criminals use capital punishment on one another.
I make it clearly emotional. I make it clearly straightforward. I claim no statistics to back up my argument. I have no desire to argue concerning whether or not it is a deterrent. I have to stand so that I represent in some way that constituency so that they can take a clear look at me. This is what they will do, and this is what they will see-a person who believes that those in his constituency of different persuasions have a right to state their case and be respected for it. But for my side I will stand firmly for
May 18, 1976

realizing that when, indeed, we decide to take life, then we have decided to go the same route as the person we are condemning. I still feel there will be those who might think that this is the soft way, that this is a way which will not serve us well.
I feel that if we were, indeed, to take lives and were to hold at our disposal the power to do that, then we would have done nothing but commit capital punishment which is what those people had committed. I cannot feel that this is correct. I cannot believe it is right. I will not accept that the only resort we have is to turn to the ultimate taking of a life and to admit that in our society we have to say it is all over, that if we get rid of that weed we will get rid of the next one that grows up.
I have heard it all before. They take the young and send them off to war. But killing does not stop killing. I think that must be said in very strong terms. I really am not interested in the comments of those who want to take life. I am really not interested in saying that they are right or wrong. I am interested in telling you that I believe I represent my own riding, the Canadian people, the young and the old, the young who represent our future and the old who represent our past. I say no Canadian government should ever again take life in the name of legality. Therefore, I will support the bill and strongly support the abolition of capital punishment.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am taking part in this debate today on behalf of the constituents of Hochelaga who elected me six months ago already. It is my first opportunity to take part in a very important debate. I shall express the views of my constituents on this very important issue, capital punishment. At the outset, let me say that I consulted the people in my riding in a sort of referendum to find out whether they favour the abolition or the maintenance of the death penalty. Out of 24,000 questionnaires sent out, I received more than 2500 replies. You will note, Mr. Speaker, that when the vote will be taken, I shall vote according to the wishes of the majority of my constituents because, to my mind, it is a way for them to take part in such an important decision.
Mr. Speaker, through my intervention, I would like to make two points: first, without repeating what all my colleagues have already said, it will of course be the matter of upholding the death penalty, but with the possibility of commuting this penalty to life imprisonment.
The second point I will deal with is prevention which in the long run will have concrete results. Of course, if we should adopt the principle that capital punishment should be maintained for the time being, such a decision would surely curb the impulses of certain individuals who will have to think about it twice before committing a crime. But, on the other hand, what might solve the problem in the long run is the second point I have just mentioned, namely prevention, but I will come back to that.
Before going any further, Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote a remark of one of constituents when he answered my referendum. That person is a retentionist who would agree to a possible commutation to life imprisonment. I will quote what he said and it should be noted with due
Capital Punishment
respect for the opinions of all other colleagues who could have a different view:
The abolitionist trend points to human dignity; the abolitionist trend seems to ignore, alas, that not only criminals but also victims are human beings and that citizens should be entitled to maximum protection since we claim to be civilized; let us see this happen in reality without being naive about it.
That is the way, Mr. Speaker, I will deal With the subject.
Let us look at the first part of my speech, that is the upholding of capital punishment. Of course, my conscience says I will not kill but perhaps we should ask ourselves the following question, namely if the one who killed asked himself that very same question. I do not know whether he asked himself that question, yet he commited a crime. So, Mr. Speaker, our first duty in this House is to make sure all Canadians have the maximum protection possible. An individual who goes into a bank or elsewhere with a gun and deliberately kills someone, knew beforehand that if he were in a difficult situation he would shoot. So we must take all appropriate means that is drastic means to protect society, just like the criminal takes drastic means to achieve his purposes. And the immediate means is the upholding of capital punishment, not in all cases, of course.
When you consider passionate crime or second degree murder, there are of course some lower degrees to consider. If someone has killed someone else, that does not necessarily make him an habitual criminal. But in many cases, he is a criminal.	*
Mr. Speaker, Canadians are presently in some way held as hostages by a minority of citizens we call criminals. I will give here some examples not to repeat what the previous speakers have said. There is the manager of a jewellery or of some business on his way to the bank for a deposit: he is attacked, shot down and falls to the ground; his assail-lant shoots him once more to make sure he will move no more. This criminal has had no thought for the respect of human life. Let us consider the child who gets killed by a bullet when a criminal gets hold of a school bus and races through a town; after a while, a shot is fired, a child is hit and killed; yet that child was not responsible, and yet he has been killed. Has this individual stopped to wonder whether to the best of his knowledge and belief he would not kill? Yet, those are things which happen and are often seen. Several examples could be found.
I can quote here also from another of my constituents and I shall read more of these comments in the course of my speech. He says this:
"A member of my family, a father of eight children, was horribly murdered for a mere $88."
Mr. Speaker, when things get so bad that people can, for minimal sums of money, take the lives of our fellow citizens, it is our duty here in this House to ensure maximum protection to the people of our country. Of course, I am willing to respect the views of those who would rather abolish capital punishment. But unfortunately, we know very well that things are pretty bad. We need only think, for instance, of organized crime. We have seen the inquiry of the Quebec Police Commission, how drugs are given to young people, how they are lured, caught and how they become total wrecks. That is crime and it is just as criminal, in my opinion, as killing somebody.

May 18, 1976
Capital Punishment
Mr. Speaker, when I was working in a hospital in Montreal before my election to the House of Commons, within six months I saw two young people of about 20 dying from absorption of mescaline. Who had supplied them that drug? It seems to me that this also is a crime, but in this case, the criminal kills by inches. Nevertheless, that criminal, the one who provides the drug, when caught, is sent to the penitentiatry for 10, 15 or 20 years maybe, but he knows he will be able to get out of there. However, he killed some people, but this is not taken into consideration. Mr. Speaker, these criminals are guilty of killing these victims of drugs. These are the ones who supplied them and I think they would deserve being hanged. Unfortunately, they are convicted for several years of mprionmnt, when we manage to catch them.
Mr. Speaker, we must bear in mind that a few years ago, when the government amended the law, we could read: "Anyone killing a policeman or a prison guardian will be hanged." Never did it happen so far. These are comments made to us by the population. They tell us: "We do not trust the government. It will not keep them in, not even for 25 or 35 years." Anyway, Mr. Speaker, what does he have to lose, the one who is convicted for 25 or 35 years, without any chance of being paroled? Killing one more person, two more, three more? He has nothing to lose. He will not feel uneasy if he gets a few extra years. This criminal has absolutely nothing to lose. Therefore, he will start again and the hazard will still be the same, and the population will no longer have any guaranty of protection.
At this stage, I would also like to mention some of the remarks made by my constituents, in my inquiry. I quote this one who is in favour of the retention of capital punishment and who says this: "Lets us get rid of hardened criminals before you and me are the next victims." Another tells us: "Now justice is encouraging crime more and more, at the expense of honest citizens who will soon have to take the law into their own hands."
Mr. Speaker, these few remarks lead one to think, and we see that people tend to have a feeling of insecurity. Today, when we go to a restaurant or elsewhere, we do not know any more if we will come out of it alive. An individual can come in, make a holdup, fire at those who are in this restaurant or elsewhere, and make a few innocent victims. However, these victims are innocent. We must consider those things and be consistent. It is our duty to warn potential murderers, through this legislation, to think it over before they decide to take another person's life, for it is up to them to choose whether they want to take the chance of being hanged. It is their own risk and their own life which will be at stake. In my view, if we elect by majority vote to retain the death penalty, we are giving the would-be criminal a warning and if he does not heed it, that is too bad for him.
Mr. Speaker, I would like now to quote from a letter which was sent to me last week by an inmate of a maximum security penitentiary. Here is what he says:
Really, I would rather be hanged ten times than serve 25 or 35 years here but on the other hand it does not make sense to me that I should get 25 years or the death penalty for murdering a policeman and only a few years for a private citizen.

Mr. Speaker, that is the testimony of a person now in detention who talks about himself. There is also the other side of the problem, that of prevention: it is the one that, in my view, should have been adopted, however, the one for which I would have voted. On the other hand, I will give my reasons later on. But before discussing that, it might be appropriate to ask each of my colleagues whether they have wondered why an individual has reached this degree of criminality. How did he get to that point? And certain examples should be given.
I am not saying that all those who are in prison have committed murders or thefts, what we call in general terms a crime, but rather I will give here an example of how a young person can come to juvenile delinquency and, eventually, to criminality, while keeping in mind the environment where he lives.
Let me give you as an example the head of a family who may be 40 or 45 years old, who has no formal education to speak of, who has just lost his job and lives off unemployment insurance while trying to find work. He cannot find a job because he does not have any diplomas, or else he is told he is too old.
Consequently, having exhausted his unemployment insurance benefits, he ends up at some point living off social welfare. That man just has to ask for welfare, and his request is complied with. He has children who are going to school and, at some point, as we know, with the high cost of living we are all aware of, the wife, who manages the family budget fairly efficiently, finds that the bills are too high for the money she gets. In time, she becomes nervous, irritable and rightly so. All of a sudden, all hell breaks loose in the family. The wife starts nagging her husband. And what does the husband do? In some cases he goes to the tavern to drown his frustrations, his problems and everything else, and the home continues to fall apart.
The child who lives in that atmosphere may be 15, 16 or 17, or even less. He goes to school and then comes a day when he wants some pocket money. What will he do? He will quit school to find work, to get a job. At some point or other, for some reason or other, he loses his job, tries to get a new one and then realizes that he does not have enough schooling. But for him going back to school is useless for he would rather work to earn some money.
Then, if he is no longer eligible for unemployment insurance, he will go to the welfare office. As soon as he gets the chance, this youngster will begin stealing here and there and he will finally get caught. Then he will be sent to prison and from that moment, mixed with habitual criminals, he will become a true criminal. This is one of the aspects of the problem. Instead of paying about $14,000 a year for a prisoner, if we had given $1,000 and $2,000 more a year to this family, not only would we have saved money, but we would have saved an individual who, instead of living an abnormal life behind bars could have lived like anyone else in society an honest and ordered life.
Mr. Speaker, we must review our social and economic policy, particularly as regards families which, in unprivileged classes, are the victims of this system. Parents cannot always be held responsible for the present situation and they did not want their children to end up that way.
May 18, 1976

Yet we have reached this point due to circumstances. Of course, Mr. Speaker, everything will not be solved overnight, but I am satisfied that through a review of our social legislation, we could substantially reduce juvenile delinquency and crime rates within the next five, ten or fifteen years. We must nevertheless be honest to the worker who is honest. Those who work for minimum wages, for instance, will be deprived of electricity or gas if they do not pay their bills. Yet the inmate does not face such problems. I do not say he is living like a king in jail, not at all.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to refer to another case on the human view point. What the individual has done is obviously illegal but what prompted him? A few years ago, a married man, the father of a number of young children who was living on welfare with a minimum income, decides at a given time to register with the Canada Manpower Centre because he does not have the education level that is usually asked for. Therefore, he gets by during a few years. He receives both welfare benefits and allowances from the Canada Manpower Centre for a retraining course.
His goal in doing so is to improve his situation, but at the same time, of course, to provide his family with a basic income of about $125 a week. Of course, after a few years, he is caught, prosecuted and accused like a vulgar criminal, being sentenced to two years for defrauding social welfare and two years for cheating the Department of Manpower and Immigration. That is four years altogether, two consecutive years for each charge, though he has only been convicted nothing more than getting payments by cheating and lying.
This individual had, of course, obtained the necessary diploma but when he was caught he was put in jail where he did a number of months and was released on parole for his good behaviour. This individual cannot find a job because he has a record so now he lives on social welfare.
Mr. Speaker, it has cost more to the state to convict him and support him in a penitentiary than if he had been forced to reimburse or to pay the fine. Of course I do not want to review the trial, because it is an example I am giving, a living example which is, in my opinion, inhuman, and for that reason I wanted to point out to what extent our social laws can sometime create circumstances in which someone is likely to commit that kind of offence and then encourage him to return to crime and live in it. Fortunately, this very individual did not go back to crime. So, Mr. Speaker, we will have to review our criminal system because there again, we can find examples which can help us understand why some individuals cannot be rehabilitated. There are several reasons for that. Even if he is rehabilitated, why is it in our present system, he has to return to crime.
I remember a former inmate told me once that the first time he went to prison, a big guy introduced himself and greeted him with both fists, stating he was the boss and not the inmate. That kind of welcome to prison certainly does not lead the way to rehabilitation. Of course I do not imply by that that all those looking after inmates act the
Capital Punishment
same way, I suppose this is only a minority and I would not like to generalize.
There is also the matter of parole. There are individuals who went out on parole, committed another offence, came back to prison and got a second parole, while another who committed one offence only, is almost rehabilitated, offers every safeguard as far as job and family are concerned without any apparent problem, he has everything to live a normal life in society but is denied parole. It is discouraging for a young fellow almost rehabilitated, when he knows another inmate goes out on parole after a second offence.
There is also the matter of parole, and I am quite familiar with that. Here is an individual who stole a car some ten years ago. After all this is not such a serious offence, he did his time, or least part of it because he went out on parole, and since then he has never committed another offence. He asks for pardon. He is married with growing children, he is an honest citizen, he wants to get a better job to ensure his family's future with higher wages, but for unknown reasons the pardon officials constantly delay the decision. Why? Mr. Speaker, in cases where offenders who are fully rehabilitated without any question meet with refusals for so small an offence, they being are being marked, they are prevented from living a decent life, they are pushed back on the way to crime. Those organizations should absolutely not be tolerated. They should be reformed, and the sooner the better in the interest not only of inmates that can be rehabilitated, but also of our institutions and the Canadian people as a whole.
There is another point that I would like to make. In certain areas, youths purchase glue in restaurants or stores. These are the youths who may become juvenile delinquents, and later on criminals. We must put a stop to this. Of course, I am not saying that tradesmen do this consciously. Young people may need glue for their school work, but I say that the government should control the glue market immediately to prevent our young people from continuing to sniff glue to drug themselves. Of course, Mr. Speaker, there will always be criminals, but when I speak about prevention and results which will be felt in five, ten or fifteen years, this is a fact, and I am certainly not alone in thinking and saying this.
If we want to considerably reduce the crime rate, prevention must start with our young people. We must invest the sum required in these young people and the groups that truly want to help young people and prevent them from becoming delinquents, to show them something different from hanging on street corners in the doorway of certain restaurants, either to smoke drugs or sniff glue or what have you.
Mr. Speaker, instead of thinking about building prisons for future needs, we should think of our youths as the men of tomorrow instead of as the criminals of the future who will fill these prisons. Mr. Speaker, before closing, I would like to tell the House that I shall vote for the retention of the death penalty, not because I want to take the life of someone else; far from it, Mr. Speaker. My first duty is to protect the majority of citizens, and to do so, I must maintain my position.
Moreover, the great majority of my constituents are for retention, and I shall vote according to the wishes of my

May 18, 1976
Capital Punishment
fellow citizens, whom I am proud to represent. I shall close on a comment of one my constituents who favours abolition of the death penalty. His comment supports what I said earlier about improving our social legislation on the one hand, and improving our penitentiary system on the other hand.
I would like to close, Mr. Speaker, by quoting the words of one of my fellow citizens from Hochelaga: The death penalty is not the only way to kill a man, he can die of a sick society.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity this afternoon to take part in the controversial debate on capital punishment, a subject we are debating while our country goes through serious times. Let me make one thing clear: I am not taking part in this debate just to let my constituents know my position, because they know my position very well. They sent a delegation to the House this afternoon. Actually, some of my younger constituents are in the gallery this afternoon.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Much has been said about capital punishment. Members have argued in favour of outright retention, retention for certain offences, and outright abolition. We have heard many statistics mentioned. You can prove almost anything with statistics. But I take another position, a position on which our constitution is based. Mr. Speaker, our constitution is based on Christian principles. I maintain that we should consider the Christian principles on which our consitution is based and see what the Scriptures have to say. Members have based their arguments on what the Scriptures say. The House has heard arguments about the deterrent aspect of capital punishment, about the need to protect society, and so on. We all want to protect society: there is no argument in that regard.
Some members have talked about punishment and retribution. To support their arguments they have quoted from the Bible passages such as: "An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth," and "Whosoever sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed." Still another passage quoted is: "He that smiteth a man so that he die, shall be surely put to death." Mr. Speaker, I insist that members who rely on the Scriptures to make their argument have not gone far enough. They stop short, not telling the House all that the Scriptures say. If one is to base one's position on what the Scriptures say, one should cite all 16 instances in which the Scriptures prescribe capital punishment as punishment for an offence. The Scriptures prescribe death for such things as adultery, cursing one's parents, false worship, and working on the sabbath-and which one of us is not guilty under at least one of these offences?
Therefore, if members want to rely on passages in the Scriptures, let them quote all pertinent passages; let them not be selective. Too often people will quote passages from the Scriptures because those passages support their position. Such people say to themselves, "This passage meets my criterion; therefore I will quote it."

We must consider the moral aspect of the question. In the end, the murderer is responsible to his Maker, his God. He is also responsible to society and the state. The state must deal with the murderer and with the criminal. The question is, how shall the state deal with the criminal, and what are the responsibilities of the state in relation to the criminal? Also, can responsibility be laid at the feet of society. I suggest that yes, society has a responsibility. We are all guilty. Therefore, let us consider the alternatives to death.
All the retentionist arguments I have heard are reminiscent of revenge. I submit that vengeance cannot be regarded as a solution to violence. True justice is devoid of any element of revenge. Unfortunately, judging from what I hear and read in the media and from what various people have said, the element of revenge colours people's thinking. I do not believe in revenge, yet constantly one hears arguments smacking of revenge. I have heard arguments about deterrence. You can support your arguments on the deterrent aspect of capital punishment with statistics, which have been used. You can talk about countries which have abolished the death sentence and compare their murder rates with the rates of countries which have retained it and, no doubt, recite most interesting figures. But I have not been able to find conclusive proof showing that the death penalty is a deterrent. I submit that it is not a deterrent. Many factors influence the murder rate in a society, factors such as our present social instability, the influence of TV-depicted violence and the increased pressures of coping in a fast-moving, technologically complex society.
The use of drugs and alcohol is a crutch when we are unable to cope. There is also the aspect of overexpenditure and gambling. You can bring all this together. When society is not able to cope, it turns to violence. The deterrent aspect has never been proven. Sir Robert Mark, commissioner of metropolitan police in London, England, spoke in Toronto recently and said:
The best deterrent to crime is the likelihood of detection followed by the certainty of conviction, rather than reliance on savage penalties unlikely to be applied in many cases because of a proper finding of guilt prevented by the operation during investigation and trial, of safeguards rightly designed to protect the innocent from a sentence of death.
He further stated:
-the continuance of the death penalty prevents the reforms necessary to increase the effectiveness of criminal justice.
I do not believe that our citizens are looking for blood. They are looking for the protection of society. As I listened to the arguments to both sides of this question I found that everyone is looking for the protection of society. We need this protection today even more than before. However, the death penalty is not a solution for the protection of society. Protection can be better achieved through revamping our judicial and penal systems. We must promote speedy arrests, certainty of arrest, speedy trials and severity of punishment. Stronger and more rigid enforcement of sentences, bail and parole laws will work better for the protection of society. This will also allow for the possibility of reform and more equitable justice than the mere act of retribution.
May 18, 1976

The protection of society can be better served by facing the problems that breed crime and violence in our society. Society will be better protected when we all face our responsibility for the type of society we have and for the elements perpetuated therein. Juries are often reluctant to convict if the death penalty is retained. They are more likely to acquit the offender. That is another reason why abolition is of greater protection to society.
We must take a positive approach. The death penalty is final and does not allow for any chance of reform or rehabilitation. Capital punishment is an irrevocable decision without any hope of redemption. A mistaken verdict can mean an irrevocable tragedy, and judicial error is always possible. This means that ultimate injustice could be performed by the state. We would be naive to believe it is very rare to sentence the innocent. Between 1889 and 1927, 50 of the 406 persons sent to Sing Sing for execution were found, upon reconsideration, to have been sentenced in error. We have moved from that day, but we still have error. Error still creeps in because we are human.
The possibility of such costly error must make one question the morality of capital punishment. There are verifiable inequities in the application of the death penalty. More often than not it is the wretched of the earth, made more pitiable by the despicable crime of murder, who become the victims of capital punishment. The well-to-do, the educated, the respectable who commit capital offences rarely forfeit their lives. While it is difficult for a rich man to get into heaven, it seems even more difficult to get him into the hangman's noose.
We have a responsibility. Imposing the death penalty avoids our responsibility and does not offer a solution to changing and correcting the problems in our society which are the source of crime and violence in the first place. Criminal behaviour is a cry for help. Society is not answering the needs; it barely hears the cry. It does not have time. We are all too busy doing our own thing and are not concerned about our fellowman. In fact, in many ways we step on him. We in society all have a responsibility for the values we adhere to and for what takes place within our human community. To simply say "yes" or "no" to capital punishments shirks our responsibility to face the problems and underlying questions of why there is crime, what are the sources or root causes and what can we do to ensure and work toward improving these conditions and preventing violence?
We must look into our homes. There is instability in our homes where our children are growing up. There is disrespect between the parents, between the parents and the children, and vice versa. We must look into our communities, school and institutions. There is disrespect for authority. This is the kind of environment in which our children are growing up. What can we expect? We can take this a little further into our employer-employee relationships. Everyone has heard the expression "work to rule". People don't seem to have any pride in workmanship any more. Where are the values that we once held so true and dear? These are some of the problems our children are facing. We must take a serious look at this and accept our responsibility. There is disrespect for law, order and authority. Each of us must examine his own responsibility. It is easy to
Capital Punishment
point the finger at the family next door-but we must look at ourselves. Are we accepting our responsibility?
What are the alternatives? There is penal, judicial and parole reform, as already mentioned, advocating strict punishment but in a more positive and productive framework. There is the question of how a criminal must pay back his debt to society. Punishment can be viewed in a more positive way by providing alternate means. A penal system must be developed where productivity and positive values are encouraged as an alternative to the negative approach to violence by sanctioning the death penalty.
The question is often asked, "What about the victim? Much has been said about the criminal, but what about the victim?" I am too practical to really worry about the victim. In fact, I say there is nothing we can do for the victim at this point. It is a fact that has been completed. As much as I might have sympathy or compassion, there is very little that can be done for the victim at this point.
But what about the families? Here is where we come in. Here is where society can help. We can offer compensation to the families affected. They should be given encouragement and assistance. Society as a whole must provide special comfort and service to the afflicted so that we all absorb the effect of the violence. We can all share in it. We can try to prevent such tragedies happening again by ensuring that the criminal is removed from society and confined appropriately, again stressing the steps to be taken to improve society and restrict those elements which harbour or perpetuate crime. Legal imposition of the death penalty does not redress the wrong done and offers no positive answer to society. Moreover, it denies any hope for the reform and rehabilitation of the criminal.
I challenge my colleagues to consider seriously the responsibility which rests upon society, which rests upon each and every one of us, and to review the decisions they have taken to date and consider supporting this bill for the abolition of capital punishment.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the fourth time I have taken part in and listened to debates in the House on this subject. It is not an easy decision to make. I think everyone has to ask himself; What is my position? He should then set it out immediately. My position is somewhat refined, in a sense, since I am a partial retentionist. I believe some form of capital punishment should be retained, and I ask hon. members to bear with me when I say "some form". Too often the principle is confused by consideration of the method of execution for planned, premeditated murder where conviction is based on direct evidence rather than on circumstantial evidence. There are many such cases and I shall refer to them.
With regard to this type of offence, I say there should be no exception. On the other hand, the Criminal Code provides for commutation in certain circumstances, and in exceptional cases where there is doubt or where any uncertainty arises at the trial-and it is always difficult to get a new hearing-it is possible for the cabinet to commute sentences, but this procedure should be used properly and always in accordance with the law.

May 18, 1976
Capital Punishment
I have in the past supported the idea that the death penalty should apply in the case of the murder of a police officer or prison guard. I also support the idea that it should apply to all persons convicted of premeditated, planned murder in cases where the verdict is based on direct evidence. Under the former terms of the Criminal Code there is a division between capital murder and noncapital murder. From my experience, I can say that defence counsel would tell the jury, before any evidence had been presented either by the Crown or by the defence, that much of the evidence to be presented would be circumstantial in nature, and in such cases the accused would be tried only on the charge of non-capital murder. I believe that system worked very well. I believe the death penalty should also apply in cases where a person is found guilty of treason, by which I mean treason in its real sense, the undermining of the country by unlawful insurrection, and that it should also apply in the case of the assassination of the monarch.
This afternoon, my right hon. friend from Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) directed a question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) with reference to the abolition of capital punishment for treason, the unlawful overthrow of the government of Canada, or the assassination of the monarch. He stated in the preamble to his question that it might be very difficult for some abolitionists to vote for a bill which contained no provision for capital punishment in such cases. I do not think anyone who knows my right hon. friend would question his philosophy on this subject-we all know where he has stood with regard to it over the years. But this is an aspect which he has questioned.
I would call the attention of the government to the fact that we are living in times when violence is on the increase, when it does seem that violent groups can get together. I do not know whether the stories we have read recently with respect to threats to the Olympics is an exaggeration or not, but we do know what happened on another occasion when the Olympics were held. I suppose the answer given by the Prime Minister was the best he could do under the circumstances. He said, to paraphrase his words, that there should not be exceptions made in particular cases. Well, Mr. Speaker, I would remind you and other members of the House that on the three occasions in recent times when this subject has been discussed in the House, he himself voted for the provision of exceptions; he voted in favour of the application of capital punishment in particular cases. In other words, on those three occasions the issue before the House was not complete abolition; it was partial abolition and partial retention.
The government undertook to give that arrangement a trial for five years. Now, 2M>
years later, we are at it again. I would point out, though, that the right hon. gentleman has commuted all the sentences passed by the courts since he became minister of justice and prime minister of the country. The situation in Canada has been one of abolition de facto, if not de jure. Members of the government have flaunted the law which they themselves developed and which was agreed to upon a vote in this chamber.
The position of the Progressive Conservative party, without any evasion or equivocation whatsoever, is that all

our members will have complete freedom of thought and action in respect of this highly controversial and emotional matter. There will be no direction given to our members by our leader. All of us will speak freely as individuals and will vote freely. On the other hand, when asked whether members of the Liberal party will be given the opportunity to vote freely, both the Prime Minister and the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) wiffle and waffle before finally admitting that though the whip will not be on as far as ordinary members of parliament are concerned, it will certainly be on for members of the cabinet.
The excuse given is that since this is a government bill, it must be supported by the cabinet. Let us consider this proposition. The government could easily make it clear that whatever way the vote should go-in particular, should it go against the government, in support of retention-it would not constitute a vote of non-confidence in the government. Then Liberal members of the cabinet as well as those on the backbenches could vote freely. Not only is there control in the sense that 27 members of cabinet will not be allowed a free vote, but influence is effectively used in other ways. In an article written during the days when this party formed the government, the prime minister talked about the power to appoint parliamentary secretaries. They were told to toe the line.
Mr. Speaker, I see it is five o'clock. I will continue my remarks after supper.

subtopic: COMMUNICATIONS
