speechtext:
I am quite prepared to let the bill go forward in the name of the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore, if that is better for them. I just think it is the type of issue that should get to committee.
The purpose of this bill, Mr. Speaker, is to amend the National Transportation Act by adding immediately after section 22(l)(i)(j) the words "provide for the establishment by all Canadian telephone companies of a universal emergency reporting telephone number". I feel a bill of this nature has a great deal of merit in light of the growing amount of emergency calls placed through the three regular means of emergency services.
A most recent example is one that took place in my constituency last Thursday. Viewers of the CBC "National" on Thursday night, May 13, will recall a clip of a shocked lady, a burned house and a demolished light plane, partially in the woman's kitchen and the rest in the backyard. This was by no means a humorous scene and it was not meant to be. One of the men in the plane was killed, the other was injured. The woman was in shock, but she managed to keep her wits enough to dial the operator. However, the line was busy. So was the police line. Finally she got through to the operator, but by that time she was very upset and could not make herself understood. Coupled with the fact of the plane crash was the woman's initial inability to get through to the operator, and by the time she did frustration had set in.
It would, of course, be presumptuous to think that a life would have been saved in this instance if an emergency telephone number had existed. What I am questioning, Mr. Speaker, is the process one faces in reporting emergencies in this country, and the subsequent delays on many occasions. Hypothetically, what if the woman's life was at stake? Would fate have waited until she had got the operator? The fact is that in many instances lives would have been saved in this country if the reporting procedure of emergencies was expedited.

May 18, 1976
Emergency Telephone Number
The woman's major complaint after this incident was the delay in getting through, and then relying on the operator to contact the proper emergency service. It is the sheer frustration that makes these critical matters worse. I firmly believe that an emergency telephone number would alleviate some of the trauma of such incidents.
This incident in Richmond, B.C., is but one isolated case; we all appreciate the fact that many more occur every day, in most cases of a more severe nature where life and death situations exist. Nearly every Canadian is aware of the British "999" exchange, while in most parts of Canada we must rely on the "0" for operator, hope the line is not tied up, and rely on her to place the appropriate call for us. This practice is not only frustrating and time-consuming, but outmoded in light of the technology the phone companies have at their disposal.
I realize that problem of jurisdiction arises in properly implementing this service. I also realize that merely making "911" an emergency number does not solve the reporting aspect of emergencies. An entire co-ordinated system is needed, and so is total agreement among involved agencies to accept the same exchange. I fully realize that boundaries of emergency agencies seldom coincide with telephone exchange boundaries or municipal boundaries. Of course, it would be imperative to have all three major services included, police, fire and ambulance.
In the interest of saving human lives and preventing disaster, I cannot foresee any hesitancy on the part of these agencies, and surely not on the part of the telephone companies. The hurdles to be cleared in instituting such a number are minimal. I think the only reason for not implementing such a number would be out of sheer disinterest and lack of compassion, not out of inability to invent the proper machinery to handle this task.
An argument against the use of an emergency telephone number is the possibility of false alarms and errors in reporting an emergency. In fact, Mr. Speaker, the telephone companies have advanced their technology to the point where there is little chance of mistake. An example is "call, hold and trace", which holds up the line the "911" caller uses. This allows the emergency bureau to ring back the caller for verification. This ensures the proper use of this number and, above all, its expeditious use. Expediency is the end goal, a character which is so sorely lacking in our present emergency system.
The 911 number is not an esoteric one. It will be used at one time or another by all Canadians in one sort of an emergency or another. The 911 number has a broad sphere of influence and I think the public will support such an innovation. More than 45 million Americans are now being served by this 911 number. Last year, in the United States, some 6.5 million calls were placed to the 911 number in New York city. It has been considered a ringing success, and the interval required for a call to be relayed to an on-scene patrol car has dropped from two minutes to 35 seconds, and in a priority call situation to less than ten seconds.
Of course, abuses will occur along the way, as they have in the U.S., and that is part of the system. But surely the positive points outweigh the negative aspects: people will, over time, acquire confidence in the system, learn to use it wisely and only in times of emergency. The co-operation of

municipal authorities will be needed, but since these same municipalities are the constitutional responsibility of the provinces, the two can get together, talk about the use of such a number and arrive at a logical and mutually agreeable arrangement.
We now have before us two other bills aimed at the protection and preservation of human life. I am sure each member is aware of the two I am referring to. Without overstating the case, I think that an emergency telephone number would have the same redeeming social value. The purpose of the bill is implicit: its sole purpose is to ensure that, if at all possible, human lives or tragedies will receive prompt attention in the face of adversity. Surely the social need for such a number overrides the jurisdictional argument.
It takes three seconds to dial 911 and over ten seconds to dial a seven-digit number. In a life or death situation, with a co-ordinated system and the 911 exchange this difference of seven seconds can in fact mean the survival of a human being. It would be a shame not to implement such a number when all the resources for such a service are at our disposal. Researchers all agree that a three-digit number can be learned and remembered by any child in the face of a crisis, but not too many will give good odds on the chances of remembering a seven-digit number. Even seven-digit numbers we dial regularly can escape us on occasion, and the chances of forgetting a long number in the face of a crisis or emergency are far greater.
Bell Canada and B.C. Telephone have both agreed to co-operate with municipalities. As for this jurisdictional and constitutional argument, no legislation is ever passed in these chambers without there being some jurisdictional difficulties. However, I hope the weight is not placed on that argument against such a number. I think those considerations should be secondary, if not tertiary, in debating the relevance of this bill.
The consequences of not implementing such an emergency telephone number in the near future, in face of the increasing rate of accidents, drug overdoses, poisonings and natural disasters, are self-evident. The gravity of this situation is too extreme to overlook the possibility of implementing such a number any longer and I would, therefore, urge hon. members of this House to allow this bill to proceed as quickly as possible to the committee so it can be discussed and passed in this House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the hon. member for following tha persistence of others in bringing forward a bill to establish a universal emergency telephone number. However, I am not going to spend almost three minutes of my speech talking about how other members are going to talk this bill out, as the hon. member did in talking his own bill out of the beginning of his speech.
I note that in the series of events the first reading of the hon. member's bill took place on October 15, 1974. The bill presented by the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson) also received first reading on October 15, 1974. The other bill referred to by the hon. member who is sponsoring this bill was presented to the House for first
May 18, 1976

reading on January 15, 1973, by Mr. Mather. Bill C-252, an act to establish a universal telephone number, was introduced by the hon. member and read the first time on October 15, 1974. The other bill was identical to the bill before us today in the name of the hon. member. These private members' bills suggest that a section be added to the National Transportation Act to provide for the establishment by all Canadian telephone companies of a universal emergency reporting telephone number. Similar bills were introduced in 1973 and 1974, and the most recent debate on this subject was in 1975.
The idea of a universal emergency telephone number appears, in theory at least, to be a very worthy one. There are a number of practical problems with the bills, however. The bills appear to be redundant in that the principal telephone carriers subject to federal jurisdiction, Bell Canada and British Columbia Telephone, have already expressed willingness to supply the service and to co-operate with municipalities in this regard. In light of the demonstrated willingness of the telephone companies to design and install a system to meet the requirements of any particular municipality, legislation would probably serve to elicit an undesirable reaction from the carriers concerned.
As drafted, the bills purport to apply to all Canadian telephone companies, whereas all the major telphone companies except Bell Canada and British Columbia Telephone are presently subject to provincial regulations.
In his speech of March 26, the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore said:
My purpose for proceeding with Bill C-252 this afternoon is not so much in the expectation that the bill will be passed, a rare occurrence in this House for legislation initiated by private members, but rather in the hope that hon. members will see fit to allow the subject matter of the bill to proceed to committee for detailed study and discussion.
He then went on to say later in his speech:
The establishment of a single emergency number through which people can summon police, fire or ambulance help in any city, not only in Canada but in all of North America, and progress in the United States has been very impressive, would be a very important step in the field of public safety. The idea is not new.
A community cannot establish a "911" emergency telphone service by simply changing over to a new telephone number. First, municipalities must be prepared to meet a number of requirements that range from resolving boundary disputes to organizing their major emergency agencies and establishing a central answering bureau. The number "911" is designed to be used for direct reporting of emergencies to an answering bureau serving a given area. The three-digit code 911 has been reserved as a universal emergency number because it is compatible with the long-range numbering plans and switching configurations of the telephone companies.
Jurisdictional boundaries of emergency agencies seldom coincide with either telephone exchange boundaries or municipal boundaries, and to avoid confusion agencies must be prepared to serve all those within an individual exchange or in exchanges having local calling with a core exchange where they may not have jurisdiction. Also, for the 911 service to be effective all three emergency services, police, fire and ambulance, should be included.
Emergency Telephone Number Mr. J. D. Cunningham, director, provincial government relations, for Bell Canada said that where telephone boundaries and community boundaries do not coincide, Bell Canada will take part in discussions to work out solutions between the affected communities. He also suggested that when a decision is made to go ahead with 911, Bell Canada will do whatever it can to assist a contracting municipality in its efforts. This could range from assistance in the development of a publicity campaign to help in training 911 operators who staff the answering bureau.
There are now seven operational 911 systems in Canada. They are operating in St. John's, Newfoundland; Fredericton, New Brunswick; London, Ontario, and in four Alberta communities. Now there is an additional one in operation in the regional municipality of Waterloo, Ontario.

speechtext: You missed Winnipeg and Brandon.

subtopic: COMMUNICATIONS

speechtext:
I am informed that I missed two. If they have them, I am glad for their sake. I might say that if we did have an emergency number which requires rapid attention, there is one number I would not hesitate to call, and that is the House of Commons number 2-4618, the number of the hon. member opposite.
I have before me a series of questions and answers that delve into this subject in a very concentrated manner. They are as follows:
1.	Why was "911" selected for the universal emergency number?
911 was selected for the universal North American emergency number because it is a brief and easily-remembered code.
It is compatible with long range numbering programs and central office switching configurations. It is also a unique number, never having been authorized for assignment as a central office or area code. In addition it is consistent in format with other System service codes such as 411 for information and 611 for repair service.
2.	What is the intent of having one universal emergency number 911? The emergency number has been offered to assist local public safety agencies in protecting the life, property and safety of the general public at the local level. It is the intent and hope that the one number 911 would apply to all emergency calls of a public safety nature in the area served since the advantages to the public depend on the universality of its use.
It should be made clear however, that the 911 number will not replace existing 7-digit emergency numbers assigned to such services as police, fire and ambulance. These regular numbers will be retained along with the facility to dial "O" operator in the event of an emergency and receive the same assistance as at present.
3.	Is Bell Canada prepared to work with key public officials in appropriate levels of government who indicate an interest in the introduction of 911 emergency service?
Yes. Bell Canada is prepared to begin working with the various municipalities and agencies who indicate an interest in planning for the introduction of the 911 emergency number. Telephone Company advice and assistance is available as required in establishing an emergency calling arrangement which effectively meets the needs of safety agencies organized to handle emergencies on a community basis from a common answering bureau.
4.	What factors should be considered in planning for the introduction of 911 emergency service?
As Company representatives begin working with the various agencies and municipalities in planning for this new emergency service, many factors which may influence the type of facilities provided, the method of operation and service dates must be taken into account. Some of the primary considerations are:
1.	the number and types of agencies to be served.

May 18, 1976
Emergency Telephone Number
2.	the number of exchanges or central office areas involved.
3.	the method used by the bureau to answer and dispatch emergency calls.
4.	the agencies' communications requirements for routine and administrative business.
5.	To qualify for the 911 service offering must a minimum number of specific emergency agencies agree to co-operate in establishing a common answering arrangement?
Yes. As a minimum requirement, emergency calls for the local police, fire and ambulance services would be included in the basic 911 service requirement.
6.	Would the central answering bureau be responsible for handling other emergency calls?
Yes. Additional emergency traffic such as medical assistance, poison control, rescue squads, etc., should also be handled through the central answering bureau. The bureau responsible for receiving 911 calls must be prepared to handle all emergency traffic from these services either by referral or transfer of the call.
The responsible agency should also agree to an appropriate method for handling any calls of non-participating agencies which may be misdirected to the 911 emergency number.
7.	Are there any special considerations necessary as to what agency, office or public official has the authority to order a 911 service arrangement?
Yes. Since 911 service required the cooperation of the local agencies such as police, fire, ambulance and others who agree to participate, the primary customer is considered to be the local or community government itself. Therefore, authority to order the service will be considered to be the governmental offices with the overall responsibility for the emergency agencies which will be included, e. g. Mayors, City Manager, Directors of Public Safety. In some cases authority may be established by acts of legislation or by resolution.
8.	In contacts with public officials and in public information programs, what are the basic points to be emphasized?
In contacts with public officials, representatives of emergency safety agencies and other interested parties, the following principles should be appropriately emphasized and demonstrated:
1.	Bell Canada is interested in providing the public with the fastest and easiest way to call for help in an emergency.
2.	A single, universal emergency number which provides direct access to an agency operated switchboard organized to handle emergencies on a community wide basis best meets this need.
3.	Bell Canada is prepared to cooperate and work with the various safety agencies and municipal officials in planning for the establishment of 911 service.
4.	Bell Canada will continue to provide "back up" emergency assistance through our highly trained operators just as we have always done.
9.	Is there a charge to the calling party for calls to the 911 emergency number?
No. In case of public telephones, a coin is presently required to obtain dial tone to complete the call. The coin is returned on completion of the call. Ideally, public telephones should be equipped to operate without the requirement that a coin be necessary to activate the dial tone. However, further work in research, design and manufacture is required to enable us to modify the range of equipment we have in service. It is therefore unlikely that we will be in a position to make a significant start on the conversion program before the end of 1970. Over 50,000 public telephones are involved.
I understand, Mr. Speaker, that that research has largely been completed.
10.	What is the Bell System position on 911 emergency service?
All Bell System companies are prepared to establish circuits that will bring 911 calls directly to a central emergency switchboard. The switchboard will be staffed and controlled by the local emergency agencies which will be responsible for making whatever response is required or appropriate to the calls. The 911 system will be supplementary to existing telephone systems and will not support either the individual telephone numbers of the various local agencies or the

service of telephone company operators when they are called upon for help in an emergency.
11.	In communities where 911 service is not yet established will Bell Canada provide for operator handling of all misdirected 911 calls on an intercept basis?
It is anticipated that the need for special 911 intercept will probably vary considerably across our territory. In some locations there may be a need to provide for it while in other instances the requirements of the municipality may be adequately met through the use of the normal vacant or re-order tones. As cost considerations will be a major consideration in the final decision together with the local requirements that will exist, specific plans will have to be developed and tailored to meet local needs.
12.	How many communication paths are required between the central office and the centralized answering position to establish a 911 community wide emergency system?
Pending the availability of local data, the number of communications paths or trunks required to initially provide 911 service will have to be determined in consultation with municipal representatives. This evaluation would give consideration to the present number of PBX trunks to police, fire, ambulance and other emergency agencies to expected emergency call volumes; to the time involved in handling typical calls; to delay at the bureau in speed of answer during peak periods, etc. Also, the municipal authorities may request separate groups of 911 trunks to assist in identifying sectors of the city placing calls.
Once the emergency bureau is activated there should be periodic review to assure that there are sufficient trunks terminating at the bureau so that on a day to day basis fully satisfactory service is provided at all times.
Will 911 service place an additional cost burden on public safety agencies?
No. Many communities are already equipped to expertly handle emergency calls from the public. The advent of 911 should not noticeably increase the volume of calls now coming in over 7-digit emergency numbers and from dial "O" for operator. Looking at the total community budgets it may be possible to save dollars by consolidating the answering functions. This has been the trend in industries that handle a large volume of calls from the general public, i.e. department stores, airlines and utility companies. Coupled with the trend toward centralization in the larger cities to accommodate more elaborate command and control systems it would be difficult to precisely evaluate the cost effect of 911.
If requested, will hold and trace or calling number identification features be available to a centralized emergency answering bureau?
Safety agencies do not now have the capability of holding on directly dialed incoming calls for tracing to determine the calling number; only calls routed through "O" Operator can be so held.
For the immediate furure, the capability to "hold" a connection to 911 for tracing is feasible ...

Unfortunately at that time my bill was talked out, but this afternoon we are provided with another opportunity to see if we cannot make some progress in what I consider to be a very important area.
The fact that this exact same bill has been debated three times in less than three years underlines a very real concern which many hon. members have about the need for a universal emergency telephone number. I believe by now all hon. members are fully aware that it was the former member for Surrey-White Rock, Barry Mather, who originally introduced this proposed legislation.
When I spoke during second reading of my bill on this subject, I pointed out the progress which was already made in the implementation of the three digit 911 emergency number in North America. I mentioned that most of this progress has been made south of the border in the United States where there are now more than 900 911 systems ranging in size from 2,000 to 8 million telephones operating and serving an estimated 30 million people.
In Canada progress has been steady, but certainly not spectacular. Winnipeg became the first North American city, in 1959, to use a three digit emergency reporting system when it cut over to 999. Brandon also uses the 999 code, but both of these communities have plans under way to convert to 911, so I am advised. At present there are eight operational 911 systems in Canada, and I mentioned those in my previous remarks.
The advantages and values of a universal emergency telephone number have been pointed out already by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta and others during debate on my bill, Bill C-252. I see no point in taking the time of the House to repeat them; however, perhaps I could read a brief note I received from a constituent who wrote to me concerning my bill. I have received quite a bit of correspondence since I tried to get the bill through, and this is just a random sampling. I will be very brief; it is just a short quote. The letter says:
I along with thousands of others, no doubt agree with this bill, and it is shameful that such necessary legislation gets kicked around by some incompetent members who have not the slightest idea of what this means or what it can afford to so many areas of this vast country. Give them-
The next word is hard to read; it starts with an H and ends with an 1.
I also have an expert from the Canadian Chamber of Commerce annual statement of policy for 1971/72 which reads as follows:
Universal Emergency Reporting Telephone Number
Since the early 1960's there has been active awareness in many communities throughout Canada of the need for a universal emergency reporting telephone number system. Indeed, some cities (for example, Winnipeg) have instituted such a system. Recognizing that the development and adoption of such a system at a national or North American level has, as yet, many unresolved problems as well as considerable expense, it is believed, nevertheless, that the need justifies and warrants its development and adoption.
Accordingly there is a recommendation which follows from this in an excerpt from the Canadian Chamber of Commerce Annual statement, which reads as follows:
That affiliated boards and chambers urge aft authorities who have jurisdiction in this matter to implement a universal emergency reporting telephone number system, such as 911 on the local, national and North American level as soon as possible.
Emergency Telephone Number I believe both these statements, one from an ordinary citizen and one from a highly respected business organization, say a lot about the need for the type of legislation which both Bill C-252 and Bill C-255 propose.
It is important to note the attitude of the Canadian Telecommunications Carriers Association toward the 911 emergency telephone system, and I have here a copy of that association's position statement dated June 5, 1974. With the permission of hon. members I would like to read it, as follows:

1.	The telephone company members of the CTCA will work with any municipality or public safety agency within Canada that is interested in establishing a centralized emergency telephone reporting centre.
2.	These member organizations believe that the development and improvement of emergency communications is in the public interest. For the sake of simplicity, effectiveness and uniformity in developing emergency reporting systems, the "911" service code is now being progressively reserved by Canadian telephone companies for this purpose.
3.	These member organizations believe that the municipality or local agency must assume the responsibility of establishing and operating the centralized emergency system. The telephone companies would be prepared to assist the local agency with technical planning and would contract to carry out the engineering and installation of the required equipment and facilities.
4.	Telephone company operators will continue to give assistance in placing emergency calls if the caller dials zero.
There are, no doubt, some real problems with regard to enacting Bill C-252 and Bill C-255. Perhaps the greatest of these problems is obtaining the necessary co-operation of the municipalities, which is basic if any universal emergency telephone number system is to be successful. However, I urge hon. members at least to agree to send the subject matter of this bill to committee for further study.

Whatever we have been or are doing in this country through emergency service, much more is going to be done in the years ahead through the citizens' band radio broadcasting, through land mobile radio transmission, through transmission of medical data, and biotelemetry. If some hon. members are familiar with the American television program "Emergency" they will know what I am referring to. Our neighbours in the United States are far ahead of us in methods of transmitting information from the scene of an accident to the hospital.
That has nothing to do with 911.

It has a great deal to do with it. If the hon. member knew the whole coverage area of the emergency medical service he would know the object is to get the equipment out into the field and transmit the medical data from the accident scene. But before you get the equipment into the field you have to get hold of it. Some people have expressed reservations about 911. First, I submit, the equipment must be available in the field. We have not become involved in this area in a major way, although moves have been made in British Columbia and parts of southern Ontario to make transmission equipment available in the field. This type of equipment should have been available long ago and we are far behind in our efforts to secure it.
We ought to be far ahead of our present position with regard to radio frequency management; we are lagging far behind in efforts to delegate bands on the radio spectrum for emergency services and in allocating frequencies for emergency uses. Also, horrendous problems can arise by virtue of the many applications of users. These we should try to avoid.
If I may return to the original point I was making before being so well led astray by hon. members opposite, I wonder if this bill is not redundant and if parliament really has power to do what the bill would purport to do. I am of opinion that the bill is redundant as telephone companies have already indicated their willingness to design and instal those systems and co-operate with municipalities and provinces in doing so. There is some question in my mind. Suppose parliament passes this bill, I wonder if it could not be found ultra vires because it purports to govern all telephone companies in the country and, with the exception of Bell Canada and B.C. Telephone, the federal government has no authority over telephone companies. The other telephone companies are all subject to provincial legislation. I think it is open to question if you can enforce this as mandatory legislation governing all telephone companies.

In the light of the new and comprehensive telecommunications legislation which it is expected will authorize the governor in council to issue directives to regulatory bodies, I submit that this kind of legislation will not be necessary. I now return to the point raised by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Brisco). I do not disagree with the provision of the 911 telephone service. I know that there would not be any great technical difficulty in providing it and that the telephone companies have shown their willingness to design and instal such a system. The difficulty will be administrative. I tell hon. members that various people in the country have brought to my attention their concerns and doubts on this question. Some disagree w'ith the installation of the 911 system. To my knowledge not everyone is in agreement with installing such a system. First we must consider questions such as manpower, staffing the central agencies which will administer the 911 system, training people in the proper operation of the system, and cost. Those questions are relevant in these times of restraint.
There is another difficulty which I think no one has mentioned, the difficulty of mistaken directions being given from a centrally administered system. For instance, in some areas cities and towns have grown up close to one another and, through accidents of history, districts and streets in different towns bear the same names. Bear in mind the difficulty which could arise. The people sitting at the central desk must give precise directions to field units. They must tell them precisely where to go. If, in two or three neighbouring towns, you have streets or neighbourhoods known by similar names, you run the great risk of sending the fire truck or ambulance to the wrong street in the wrong town. Such mistakes can be serious because you could lose an hour, whereas local units would know exactly where to go.
I have heard no one talk of volunteer services, volunteer fire companies and volunteer emergency service brigades which now serve in local areas but are not professional. subtopic: SETTING OF PRICES FOR OIL AND GAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government has today reached certain major decisions concerning crude oil and natural gas prices and I wish to communicate them to the House.
The current arrangements for oil and gas pricing expire on June 30. For some months past the government has been in the process of discussion and negotiation with provincial governments, seeking to reach agreement on the prices which should prevail under new arrangements to come into effect on July 1. Among the various efforts to reach agreement have been the federal-provincial conferences on energy on December 12 and March 5, the meeting of first ministers on May 6, and numerous bilateral contacts at ministerial and first ministers level.
Since the meeting of May 6 the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has spoken personally with nine of the premiers and with the deputy premier of Saskatchewan. The announcements I am about to make are in large measure the result of these intergovernmental efforts to find the best possible solution.
As hon. members are aware, the single price for crude oil in Canada has, since last July, been held at $8 per barrel. This is about $4.50 below the international price which now prevails. As I said in the House on April 27 when I tabled the document "An Energy Strategy for Canada- Policies for Self-Reliance", Canada has been more fortunate than most countries. Because we have domestic reserves we have been able to cushion the effects of higher international prices. However, as I also pointed out, our reserves of oil and natural gas are declining and we now import more crude oil than we sell abroad. Finding and developing new reserves will cost far more than in the past, and we will have to pay higher prices now to bring about the exploration necessary to achieve self-reliance in the future.
At the energy ministers conference in March I suggested that the lowest increase in crude oil prices that could be considered would be $1.05. That is the amount by which international prices rose last year, and an increase of that amount in Canada is needed simply to restore the differential between Canadian and international prices which had been worked out and agreed upon by the Government of Canada and the producing provinces a year ago. But I also suggested that an upper limit be set, of not more than a $2 increase, bearing in mind the effects any increase has on inflation and on the capacity of Canadian industry to compete in world markets. Within that range from $1.05 to $2 I stressed the continuing policy of the government that the Canadian price must over time move toward interna-
May 18, 1976

tional prices if our long-term energy objectives are to be met.
In the discussions with the provinces it has been natural for the producing provinces, which own the resources, to press for higher prices for oil and gas to ensure themselves the best possible revenues to compensate them for the loss of their depleting assets. At the same time they have recognized the effects of price increases on the economy of all of Canada.
Governments of consuming provinces have, naturally, been mindful of the effects the price increases would have on their consumers. At the same time they have had to consider the claims of producing provinces for recognition of their rights as owners of the oil and gas. The Government of Canada has had to keep all of these factors in mind, and particularly that most difficult dilemma, the fact that price increases in these major commodities would add to inflation but, at the same time, the fact that if we did not increase prices we would be jeopardizing our future energy supply.
In the light of all these considerations, the government has now reached the following conclusions: first, there should be a standard "freeze" period on petroleum product prices of 60 days across Canada which would run from the date of any increase in crude oil at the well-head. Prices to consumers would not, therefore, rise until 60 days from the date of the authorized increase in the prices producers receive for crude oil.
Second, the price of crude oil in Canada should rise by $1.05, that is to say, from $8 to $9.05 on July 1, 1976, and by a further 70 cents to $9.75 on January 1, 1977. Consumers would not begin to feel the effects until after 60 days from these dates.
Third, the price of natural gas should rise by 15.5 cents at city gate Toronto, that is, from $1.25 to $1.40.5 per million B.T.U's on July 1, 1976, and by a further ten cents to $1.50.5 on January 1, 1977. I should note that with these price increases natural gas will continue for an additional year to retain its approximate 85 per cent commodity price relationship with crude oil.
Fourth, export prices on natural gas will also increase. The government is now reviewing a report on this subject from the National Energy Board and is discussing the situation with representatives of the government of the United States. We hope to be able to make an announcement concerning the amount and timing of the increase within a month. For the three producing provinces, Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia, we think we can get agreement but will have to await their response. That response may well be influenced by the conclusions which are reached in the next few weeks concerning export prices. The decisions I have just reported to the House would seem likely to carry with them, therefore the acceptance not only of the federal government but of the majority of producing and consuming provinces in Canada.
In making this announcement I would like to confirm that despite differing views among the provinces as to the ideal "freeze" period, all have accepted the 60-day period that will now be adopted in connection with the coming increases.
Oil and Gas Prices
On the vital question of oil and gas prices, we do not have full agreement between all governments across Canada. A few provinces cannot bring themselves to acknowledge the need for these higher prices but we believe, based on our discussions, that a good majority will do so.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. gentleman for his statement on oil pricing. It comes as a result of a great deal of discussion and argument between producers and consumers and there is little doubt as to the winner of that particular debate for it is apparent that, having obtained the $9.75 price per barrel this year, the government will go on to the $13 barrel in a very short space of time, with related increases in the price of natural gas in both the domestic and export markets.
First, let there be no question that this is one increase of $1.75, not two smaller increases, as far as the inflationary impact is concerned. At a time when wages and salaries are being held back it will be hard to justify what is in reality an arbitrary price increase to the Canadian public. To people locked into existing patterns of energy consumption, often through no fault of their own, it will be a bitter pill to swallow.
The problems faced by many who live in Atlantic Canada are especially germaine. In Nova Scotia for example, electricity prices have gone up during the past year by rates in the order of 70 to 80 per cent. Another 10-20 per cent is sure to cause hardship. No one denies the need to help people locked into this crushing spiral except the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie). Today he has followed up his now notorious statement of May 4 with yet another blow to their well being. Let us hope the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) in his budget next week recognizes their problem by introducing meaningful tax relief for low income groups, or some other type of special compensation.
It has become clear with the release of the energy strategy document that the government has only one energy policy, and that is price. There is no real policy on energy conservation. There is no real policy on the development of renewable resources of energy. There is no real policy of federal-provincial energy	relations-this	unilateral
increase demonstrates that in no uncertain fashion.
Since the price is to rise, it must be to increase revenues flowing to exploration. The record shows that in the past this has not happened. Between March, 1974, and November, 1974, the price rose by $2.70 cents; the industry share decreased by 8c. Between November, 1974, and the present day the price rose by another $1.50; the industry share rose by 43 cents. The rest went in tax, which today accounts for two thirds of the price of domestic oil.
The fact is that the government's pricing of oil, outside as it is of any coherent energy policy, has nothing to do with energy-only with increasing the federal government tax take. The tragedy which faces all the people of Canada who are now locked into an outdated, punitive, ill advised process is that the government has yet to recognize that it is the rate of return on investment-not prices-which is critical for the generation of oil exploration in this nation.

Oil and Gas Prices
Filling the coffers of a profligate government surely ought not to be the cornerstone of a rational energy policy.
The Minister has said that if exploration proceeds according to plan 50 cents of each dollar increase will go to the development of our energy reserves. If the energy strategy is not to become just one more piece of dubious government optimism it may well have to cede a greater part of its oil revenue to the producers.
We in the opposition cannot accurately judge the efficacy of this latest move in the absence of the information available to the planners at the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. Is the hon. gentleman prepared to release the data behind his projected exploration cash requirement? Will he explain the macro-economic impact of his proposed hike and let us know the current estimated cost of developing all frontier energy resources? Will he inform us as to the effect of a price hike in qualitative terms on energy conservation?
In addition, we must have detailed information about the price freeze which the government intends to impose. In the so-called energy strategy document, a number of freezes on product prices are discussed. The government's own recommendation was for 45 days; the commissioners of the province of Ontario recommended 30 and 40 days during the last price hike. Why is 60 days now suggested?
Once again Canadians are treated to an ad hoc, uncorrelated statement on energy. The credibility of the government in this field when judged by almost every standard seemed to reach an all-time low when a former minister of energy, mines and resources stated in a famous speech at Denver, Colorado, a few years ago that Canada had enough oil to last for centuries. The present minister, with his recent statement on energy strategy and his inability to work out an integrated energy program with the provinces, is surely challenging his predecessor's record of ineptitude.

subtopic: SETTING OF PRICES FOR OIL AND GAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, ever since the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) announced that it was the government's intention to move toward the world price of oil the public of Canada have been expecting there would be periodic increases. However, a punch in the jaw does not hurt any less simply because one has seen it coming. One of those blows was struck tonight in the announcement the minister has just made increasing the price by $1.75 a barrel.
The two increases, which must be taken together, represent a very serious imposition on Canadian consumers. The higher price means that those who are driving cars will have to pay an additional 5 cents a gallon. Of course this could be offset if the government were prepared to cancel its 10 cents a gallon excise tax when the budget comes down. But assuming the government is not in such a generous mood, this increase of 5 cents a gallon will mean an extra $40 or $50 a year for the average family.
The increase in the price of natural gas is to be 25 cents per thousand cubic feet which, if one is heating a home with gas, represents some $43 or $44 a year in additional cost, and about $42 per year if one is heating a home with oil.
The impact of the increase in the price of oil alone will add to the burden on Canadian consumers to the extent of

some $1,300,000,000 a year, and the increase in the price of natural gas will create a substantial additional burden.
These increases that the minister has just announced will boost the consumer price index in Canada by at least two percentage points. At a time when the cost of living is still rising, when the workers of this country are being urged to exercise restraint, I would ask the House how long the people of Canada can be expected to accept this growing acceleration in the cost of operating their cars, heating their homes, operating their farm machinery, and running their fishing boats. This is particularly so today when the government is seeking to hold down the incomes of the working people.
One must recognize that with our diminishing supply of oil and gas resources it is necessary to face the fact that prices must move upwards. On behalf of the New Democratic Party may I say we see no justification at all for any increase in the price of oil and gas unless there is an iron clad assurance that the increased revenue will go into exploration for oil and gas in order to assure the Canadian public of supplies of these commodities in the future. To date the government has given no such iron clad guarantee.
Every time that the minister and any of his colleagues make a speech about the necessity for increasing the price of oil and natural gas, they put forth the argument that the oil industry must have an increased cash flow. In other words what they are saying is that the consumer must not only pay for the barrel of oil that he or she buys, but must also put up the money to find another barrel of oil or gas to take its place. This is what I have characterized as the "pay now and then pay later" syndrome.
I think the Canadian people would understand and accept the argument that it is necessary to increase the price of oil in this country so as to accumulate the necessary capital to find more oil, provided they could be assured, first of all, that this money would be used to find oil, and secondly, that when oil was found they would be able to buy it at reasonable prices, not at whatever price the oil cartel chooses to charge them. The fact is, of course, that there has been no such assurance. In the last three and a half to four years the price of oil has moved steadily from $2.75 a barrel to $8, not so much because the cost of production has gone up but because it has been argued that the oil companies needed the additional money to do exploration work.
What are the facts, Mr. Speaker? The facts are that the amount of money spent on exploration as a percentage of the oil companies' earnings has declined, not increased. At the present time any increase in the price of oil will go to the treasuries of provincial and federal governments and to the oil industry. There is no guarantee that either levels of government, federal or provincial, or the oil industry will use this $1.75 a barrel increase on oil exploration- which is the only justification there can be for increasing the price.
The members of this party have been arguing, as has the government of the province of Saskatchewan, that any increase in the price of oil should be put into a national resources fund. This money will go to the oil companies, as

well as into the federal and provincial treasuries, whereas the entire $1.75 a barrel and any other increases that follow should go into a national resources fund. The money could then be paid out to those oil companies that actually do some exploration. Money could also be made available to provincial governments that are prepared to use a government agency to do exploration and development. It could also be used to finance Petro-Canada to do a genuine job of exploration and development in Canada, so that the people of Canada might own an oil company that will explore for and produce oil at a reasonable figure, instead of being held up, as they have been for all the years that most of us can remember, by the international oil cartel.
We therefore regret that the government has decided to raise the price of oil in two jumps to $9.75 a barrel without bringing in any program whatever to assure Canadian consumers that the additional $1.3 billion that is going to be taken out of their pockets will be used to find oil for the years ahead. Unless the government is prepared to take steps to assure the Canadian people that the extra revenue that they will have to put up is going to be used for exploration and development, I think the Canadian people will look upon this increase as just another attempt at the kind of rip-off that we have ever since the price of oil has gone from $3 to $8 a barrel.

Mr. Speaker, before opening my remarks on the minister's statement, I would like to emphasize a point that we have made many times but which does not seem conducive to tangible results. I think it should be realized once and for all that we are fed up with playing second fiddle, which means that when a minister has a statement to make, he should have the decency to table copies of it in both French and English, simultaneously. The excuses which are regularly presented are nothing more than a balm poured into a wound which keeps being inflicted on us. This being said, Mr. Speaker, we hope the matter is stettled. To come back to the declaration as such, let me first state that we are not sure of the provinces' response to the government's decision.
I say this because a direct agreement among the provinces might be a better answer than this unilateral decision made by the minister.
I also wish to mention the very important and very surprising contradiction in the attempt made to justify higher oil prices. They justify this increase by saying it is to avoid a shortage, to encourage a continuing oil production.
Mr. Speaker, let them explain how rising oil prices will increase our supplies. I do not dig it. This phenomenon should be explained to us once for all. I should like to understand. How does a higher price for a barrel of oil increase the oil energy potential in Canada? I wish to get a good explanation because, as the previous speaker just said, every oil company in Canada spends-and always did-a good part of its revenue for the discovery of new fields and new wells. It is something normal. We do not have to supplement their effort in that field. If they do not do it, they do not perform their duty.
But we agree to help in some ways to encourage exploration. However, Mr. Speaker, I think they are going too far
Oil and Gas Prices
when they try to convince us that Canadians ought to pay more if we are to increase our oil supplies. It is inaccurate. It is absolutely wrong. And furthermore each time we talk about energy we are told that oil and natural gas supplies are diminishing. If it is true will it be different with an oil price increase? I ask for proof. And the fact is that we now import more crude oil than we sell to foreign countries.
It is always ridiculous when a government, a minister tells us at the same time that our oil supplies are dwindling and that we are selling oil abroad. It is stupid. Our reserves are declining and to develop them, we have to pay a higher price for a barrel of oil. We wonder how this can happen, but indeed, this is what the minister tells us.
And moreover, we import more oil than we sell. But how stupid and ridiculous it is to go on selling if our reserves are running out; the government should have stopped long ago selling oil to foreign countries, with the threat of a shortage of oil in its own country. There are discrepancies that must be rectified. When the minister says, at page 3 of the declaration I have before me:
... the Canadian price must over time move towards international prices if our long-term energy objectives are to be met.
What a pity! If those are long term objectives we want to achieve, that is, bring by miracle or whatever means more oil than we now have in Canada through our own natural resources, then once again we have to know exactly what this means. We are therefore against purely artificial increases, just for the sake of increasing, on the grounds that this will bring more oil into Canada.
We do not accept that. We would like to have a lot more details. We are in favour of producing provinces having a more adequate, greater income. But then I say it is a lot less the role of the federal government than of the provinces among themselves. Let there be agreements between Quebec, for example, and Alberta for the purchase of items Quebec needs, let the two provinces do it directly at a mutually agreed price.
I think that would be more normal than the intermediary role set for the federal government, particularly when one thinks about the arguments put forward, stupid arguments, saying we are going to save our oil by raising prices, saying there is a shortage which will disappear if the price is increased. That, Mr. Speaker, we are not prepared to accept. We will have to be given a little more scientific and truer arguments to believe that. In the meantime, we are quite simply opposed to any artificial increase in prices.
If Canada can have energy at a cheaper price than elsewhere it is up to us to avail ourselves of that opportunity, to glorify Providence for it and not run after an escalation in prices on the pretence of reaching international prices. We must be mature and adult enough to act responsibly, even if the Constitution is still in London.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Allmand that Bill C-84, to amend the Criminal Code in relation to the punishment for murder and certain other serious offences, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before debate on the bill was interrupted by private members' hour I said that I was in favour of capital punishment for some offences. I favoured its retention in cases of planned, premeditated murder where the conviction was based on direct evidence rather than circumstantial evidence. I also suggested it should be retained for treason, and spoke about unlawful attempts to overthrow the government, insurrection, and assassination of the monarch. In all those cases we ought to consider imposing capital punishment.
According to certain newspaper reports the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has indicated to certain backbenchers that they had "better get with it", meaning that they had better support the bill, or else! I hear and suspect that the cabinet will vote en bloc in favour of the bill, and that parliamentary secretaries too will vote en bloc. They are all looking for promotions, for appointments to judgeships, and so on. The Prime Minister made his meaning clear to backbenchers. The plums are there, to be given out as appointments. The retentionists will not be given the plum posts, the judgeships, the highly paid positions on regulatory boards, and so on. This is understood among hon. members opposite.
Let me say a word about convicted murderers of policemen and prison guards now serving time. The list in my hand goes back to June, 1973. Who are these men who have been so convicted? They include John Francis Connearney, who was convicted of killing a police officer in Quebec; John Harvey Miller, convicted of killing a police constable at Surrey, British Columbia; Rene Vaillancourt, convicted of killing Constable Leslie Maitland of Toronto; Real Char-trand, convicted in November, 1972, of killing a constable in Quebec. It also includes George Joseph Peloquin, who was convicted of killing a carpentry instructor at Stony Mountain penitentiary. It includes James Lawrence Hutchison and Richard Joseph Ambrose, who were convicted of killing a police constable and a corporal at Moncton, New Brunswick; Elery Steven Long, who was convicted of killing a staff-seargeant at Delta, British Columbia; and Gilles Hebert, convicted of killing a prison guard at Archambault Institution. I can recite many more names, Mr. Speaker. The list in my hand says little about the victim. We hear little talk of the victim but hear much talk about convicted men.
Let me now deal with the Solicitor General's (Mr. Allmand) speech and consider his arguments. He told us that he has participated in three previous debates on capital punishment, and said that hon. members who have been here for ten years, as he has been, will be participating in
May 18, 1976

their fourth full-scale debate on capital punishment. On three previous occasions the Solicitor General voted in favour of partial retention, that is, retention for certain offences only; each time the government had proposed the bill, and each time the government persuaded dissident backbenchers to support it.
The Solicitor General went on to talk about the question of objectivity. He said that if we consider this question objectively then we must, from a logical, ethical and public policy point of view, conclude that capital punishment must be abolished once and for all. I ask what are these logical, ethical, and public policy points of view? If it was unethical to vote for partial retention last time and twice before that, is the Solicitor General admitting that he voted against his own ethics, his own ethical inclinations? Remember, Mr. Speaker, the definition of public policy is always subject to interpretation. If it means public concern and public will, I think every constituency in Canada would vote overwhelmingly in favour of retention of capital punishment for some offences, particularly at this time when murder and violence are on the increase.
Let me illustrate what I mean. I sent out about 38,000 questionnaires asking people if they are in favour of capital punishment in cases of planned, premeditated murder. Of those who replied, 6,320 were in favour of retaining capital punishment for some offences; only 676 voted against capital punishment. I submit that any accurate report of the feelings of constituents all over the country would show that most of them would vote in the same way as those who answered my questionnaire. If polls could be taken in Vancouver, Edmonton, Winnipeg, Toronto, Montreal, Halifax or Moncton, the results would be much the same, I submit, as in my survey.
The Solicitor General maintains that the death penalty is no deterrent to the commission of murder. But he has no evidence to support his argument. Let him explain to the House why reported murders increased from 315 in 1968 to 545 in 1974, an increase of almost 60 per cent. This increase has occurred while the Solicitor General, and the government he supports, have been playing yo-yo with the subject in parliament.
In one year, 1974 to 1975, the murder rate increased 18.8 per cent, or at about the same rate as inflation. I point out that just recently Dr. Fattah was paid a big fee to produce a report on the subject of capital punishment. I do not criticize him; he is a professor, and was an abolitionist when he obtained his doctorate. He remained on abolitionist when he was hired to write a report. He produced a report which argues in favour of abolition. And what does that mean? It means nothing at all. It simply means that when he wrote the report, he followed his conscience and argued that the death penalty should be abolished. But he ignored the increase in murder.
Let me quote some figures to illustrate the recent murder rate. They are interesting. There were in 1961, 185 murders; in 1968 the figure jumped to 315, and by 1974 to 545. As I said previously, in a very short space the murder rate increased 60 per cent. The population did not increase by 60 per cent in the same period. And, as I said, in the 1974-75 period the murder rate went up more than 18 per cent. How can the Solicitor General maintain his position?
Capital Punishment
The practical question is not whether the death penalty would deter the would-be murderer, but whether it would deter him more than life imprisonment would deter him. Giving a capital murder convict 25 years in a penitentiary is certainly not going to deter murder. It is going to endanger the lives of every warden, police officer, and person in the correctional service in Canada. That is what it is going to do. Once you have been sentenced to 25 years, what do you have to lose? I might just pause here.
When these two tourists from Vancouver, one charged with murder and the other attempted murder, came to Calgary, they robbed a credit union, shot a police officer, and then holed up in a house with two girl hostages. They said to the police through their communication that they had nothing to lose.
We talk about humanity, but if a man 52 years of age is sent to jail for 25 years, he will not get out until he is 77. During that time will he be kept in solitary confinement in order to protect all the officers, guards, and wardens? I predict that if the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) stays in that position long enough, he will revert to the old system where such prisoners are let out on parole. We already know of people who have committed murder for the second time. It does not matter if they do it three or four times again, they cannot get more than 25 years.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: They will not stay there.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
I agree. Then there is the argument that there is more sympathy and more feeling for the person who commits deliberate murder than there is for the victim. The hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) talked about a fellow who shot a policeman in the arm. When the policeman fell down by a car, the fellow said that he had everything to gain from shooting him and then shot him through the eyes. That is the kind of psychology there is today.
I have a lot of experience as a defence lawyer. What concerns me is that murder is becoming socially acceptable. No one gives much thought to a person who commits a petty theft such as shoplifting. That is almost acceptable. Therefore you kill somebody.
I listened to an hon. member speaking this afternoon. He said, "What can you do about the victims; they are dead and buried." The murderer may have on his record more people who are dead and buried. What protection is there for society? Canadians are concerned.
The Solicitor General said it is more difficult to get a conviction when we have the death penalty. In my opinion, and I do not want to be unkind to him, that statement bears no relationship to the facts. I question whether he has had a jury trial on a capital murder case. I find that a jury will take the facts, whether they be from direct evidence or circumstantial evidence, weigh them, and come to a conclusion. In my formula, of course, I would not use the death penalty on circumstantial evidence. If it is circumstantial evidence the jury will likely go the other way.
Is the minister suggesting that we get rid of the death penalty because it is hard to get a conviction? Is he suggesting he wants a conviction in order to put these people

May 18, 1976
Capital Punishment
in jail for 25 years? Is that his position? I listened to him on the Monday night, but I still do not know.
There is talk about judicial error. Under the old law, judicial error was a valid argument. However, today, murder is divided into capital murder and non-capital murder. Capital murder was always interpreted under the Code before it was moved, changed, repealed, and amended. The judge who would draw the charge of capital murder would instruct the jury that they could find a reference of non-capital murder. Therefore the question of judicial error is not an argument. It might have been an argument 25 years ago before the amendments were made to the Code.
We have the security package. Part of the security package is the gun control law which seems to get more airing than the last part, and legalizing provincial inquiries which the Supreme Court of Canada says are already legal. They are now bringing in amendments to undo what they did in reference to wire tapping. No notice is necessary. I have said over and over again that if a police officer is not going to give notice to the subject that his telephone will be tapped, he should get leave from a judge, and then only under exceptional circumstances. Police officers I have talked to admit that they have not really tried a judge in this regard and therefore cannot say whether they have faith in that system.
All this was done for one purpose, to get people off the track. It always puts you in mind of a political tactic. When you go to a pond in the spring, you may see some mallard ducks. If the female has some ducklings, instead of swimming away she will make it appear as though she has a broken wing or leg in order to lead you away from the slough. This is what the government is trying to do, take people's minds off the economics of the country and the problems facing us today.
When you are dealing with the control of crime you need three things; quick detection, swift apprehension, and proper punishment. I used this example on other occasions when dealing with the question of deterrents.
When there is talk about whether the death penalty is a deterrent I often use this illustration. There is a rock in a harbour and upon it a lighthouse is placed to warn ships of the danger. One hears about the ships that run upon the rock in the fog, or during a storm, but one never hears of the ships that passed by in safety.
In a day in which we have high unemployment, inflation because of over-extravagant spending by the government, coupled with almost an illegal increase in the amount of currency, wage and price controls, threats by the national unions of Canada that they will organize and have a national strike from coast to coast, an increase in crime in every field, the government, within two and a half years of debating capital punishment, brings it in again to distract the minds of the Canadian people from the real problems and, above all, fails to carry out the death penalty.
A former prime minister used this quote. I dug it up to use it today. This is what Cromwell said about a parliament. This quote was used by the late Lester Pearson when he was Leader of the Opposition. He said to the then government, and I quote:

You have sat there too long for the little good that you do. It is time to make way for better men. In the name of God-go.
For following the tactics it is using, that is what I say to this government.
